title: The future of New Orleans jazz
summary: Green and the interviewer discuss young players, recordings and survival of the music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Um, how do you feel about the future of this music in general? I mean, as we know in New Orleans, the younger, younger people in New Orleans really aren't thinking out of music. Um, how do you feel about the future in general? Not necessarily for the rest of it.

Mixed, mixed feelings, Tom. Uh, I think it's such a specialized art form it can get away from you unless you hear it and play it as often as possible. I think the tendency, there is, in any band, there's a tendency for a band to disintegrate, less ensemble and more solo. Uh, all over the world, really largely through George, uh, and the recordings, uh, young bands are playing New Orleans style. How deeply rooted this is, I don't know. You see, it isn't this present generation. It isn't the men between 40 and 50 who are playing now. It's, who's gonna come afterward. You see a boy like young Tom Sancton, who played at George's Wake, playing this incredibly beautiful George Lewis style clarinet. It gives you great hope. But I wonder who young Tom Sancton will be playing with in another 20 years.
And we might say here that, uh, Tom Sancton is from New Orleans, which is quite unusual.
That's right. New George, you heard him. Uh, what happens in another 20 years? I don't know.

Of course, we have bands like the Hall Brothers Band in Minneapolis, which are a young band, and they're playing, uh, I think very well in New Orleans style. Beautiful. Beautiful. Of course, there are really very few, it's almost the only band in the country that was in that class.
In England, you have Sammy Remington, superb musician. Beautiful George Lewis clarinet. Beautiful sax.

Well, actually I feel that it's hard to believe that music of the quality of New Orleans as I discussed, which I think is a very high quality, can really die out. I mean, I think there must always be people with sufficient musical, um, sensitivity to realize this is something quite exceptionally good. And one feels, perhaps optimistically, that it's got to survive somehow. I don't know.

I think now the chance is better than it was after the first, quote, death of New Orleans jazz, because it's on LP records and it's beautifully recorded and it's available, which was not true in 1945, when George and Bunk came back. So that this music has been so documented that it is possible now to imitate from the music and to grasp it from the music rather than just hearing it in person. So I, there, there's a legacy now that's been recorded and I think it's important.

If George, in a sense, does have pupils, and I had never actually studied personally under him, there are people who have, who have studied memory on his records, which, uh, I think means that he should, by all odds, continue to have quite a considerable influence.
But whether he will have the, the, the drummers and the piano men, uh, and the trombones and the, and the horns to back him, I don't know. I hope so. And I think so.
